To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the mixed models approach to the analysis of data in which both participants and stimuli vary is a comprehensive solution to the problem of treating stimuli as a random rather than fixed factor, that the failure to use mixed models in the analysis of data from experiments that involve stimuli as a random variable is a serious and pervasive problem, and that the failure to take account of the random nature of stimuli can have substantial effects on the conclusions that are reached about the data.

the use of traditional analysis of variance (ANOVA) procedures for the analysis and interpretation of data with both participants and stimuli as random factors can be seriously misleading, and that mixed models offer a comprehensive and powerful alternative.

(1) ignoring either participants or stimuli in the analysis of data from experiments with crossed random factors is a serious error, (2) mixed models are an excellent solution to this problem that has long plagued the social and cognitive sciences, and (3) mixed models are now readily available for the analyses of data from experiments that include crossed random factors, and they can be used in the analysis of virtually any data set.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the proper analysis of social psychological data when stimuli are treated as a random factor.

the analysis of social psychology experiments in which the experimental stimuli (or treatments) are treated as random variables, and we show that the standard approach to the analysis of such data is flawed.
the analysis of data in which both participants and stimuli have been randomly sampled from populations.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the mixed models solution is the only correct solution to the problem of treating stimuli as a random variable.
mixed models provide a comprehensive and detailed solution to the problem of treating stimuli as random factors in social psychology.
the use of the mixed model approach to data with crossed random effects is the best available solution to the problem of treating stimuli as a random effect.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

mixed models are a powerful tool for social psychologists who are interested in the effects of experimental stimuli, and we hope that this work will encourage more social psychologists to use mixed models in their work.
mixed models are a powerful, flexible, and easy to implement tool that can help to solve the pervasive problem of ignoring stimuli in social psychological research.

the mixed models approach provides a solution to the problem of ignoring stimuli that is superior to all other approaches, including the use of random effects models that treat stimuli as a fixed factor.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the mixed model approach to the analysis of data from social and cognitive psychology is a simple, powerful, and flexible tool that can be used to address many of the problems that are inherent in the analysis of data that are collected with stimuli that are sampled from a larger universe of possible stimuli.

, when participants are sampled randomly from the population and stimuli are also sampled randomly from the relevant population, the analysis of the data must take into account both the participant and the stimulus random factors.

the failure to treat stimuli as random factors can result in substantial and potentially serious errors in the estimation of effects of theoretical interest, and that mixed models provide a comprehensive and powerful approach for the analysis of such data.
